title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Institutional Flow & Momentum Setup
book_title: Chapter 8: Reading the Tape — Trend, Volume & Momentum Opportunity

epigraph.quote: Never buy a stock or ETF in Stage 4, no matter how cheap it looks; a falling 30-week moving average is a ceiling of trapped supply, not a bargain basement.
epigraph.author: Stan Weinstein, Secrets for Profiting in Bull and Bear Markets

web_blocks.html: On Stan Weinstein's Stage Analysis framework, KORU is unambiguously in Stage 4 (Declining Phase) as of November 13, 2026 [8]. Closing at $7.68, KORU sits -69.66% below its 30-week SMA ($25.31), -68.11% below its 200-day SMA ($24.08), -51.55% below its 50-day SMA ($15.85), and -43.45% below its 10-week EMA ($13.58) [8]. Even its short-term 10-day ($8.45) and 20-day ($10.02) moving averages are sloping downward above price, acting as immediate overhead resistance [8].

Equally important, the unleveraged benchmark EWY ($142.78) sits in Stage 1 (Basing), sitting -18.61% below its 30-week SMA ($175.43) and -15.24% below its 50-day SMA ($168.46) [9], while FLKR ($47.36) is likewise in Stage 1 (Basing) below its 30W SMA [20]. Meanwhile, the broader US equity market is in a Correction regime (S&P 500 below its 50-DMA, 47.6% breadth above 50-DMA, 42.9% breadth above 200-DMA, and 6 distribution days over the last 25 sessions). Neither the underlying Korean index nor the US macro tape supports high-beta leveraged long exposure right now.

web_blocks.html: In the options market, KORU carries an IV_CHEAP label only in a relative sense: ATM implied volatility is 136.9% against a staggering 224.1% 20-day historical volatility [8]. However, cheap relative IV in a Stage 4 falling knife is a classic value trap for call buyers, because theta decay burns premium while price drifts sideways or lower. As the deterministic Options Playbook below shows, the options stance is strictly WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT_OR_BASE—stand aside at $7.68 and never deploy capital until a $6.28 base stabilizes or a Stage 2 breakout forms.

web_blocks.html: What would it take for KORU to become technically investable again? First, the underlying index proxy EWY ($142.78) must halt its decline, carve a multi-week horizontal Stage 1 base, and reclaim its 30-week SMA ($175.43) [9]. Second, KORU itself must stop printing lower lows below $6.28, allow its 10-week EMA ($13.58) and 50-day SMA ($15.85) to flatten and turn upward, and break out on volume exceeding 1.5x its 30-day average (45.26M shares) [8]. Until every one of those prerequisites is met, bottom-fishing KORU is pure speculation.

Cross-checking KORU's technical posture against the broader US market regime reinforces the discipline of patience. With the S&P 500 trading below its 50-day moving average, breadth at 47.6% above the 50-DMA (42.9% above the 200-DMA), and six distribution days logged in the trailing 25 sessions, institutional risk budgets are actively contracting. In such regimes, leveraged single-country ETFs with 8.53 effective beta and 224.1% 20-day realized volatility [8] experience forced de-grossing regardless of local Korean earnings multiples.

book_paragraphs: If Chapter 7 explained the math of why KORU can lose money even in an up year for Korean stocks, Chapter 8 reads the tape to tell us where we stand right this second. Open the weekly and daily charts of AMEX:KORU as of November 13, 2026, and there is zero ambiguity. KORU is deep inside Stan Weinstein's Stage 4 declining phase. At a closing price of $7.68, the fund is trading 43.45% below its 10-week EMA ($13.58), 51.55% below its 50-day SMA ($15.85), 68.11% below its 200-day SMA ($24.08), and 69.66% below its 30-week SMA ($25.31).

When an instrument sits nearly 70% below its 30-week moving average, every single rally attempt runs straight into a wall of trapped buyers desperate to get out near breakeven. Look at the short-term moving averages too: the 10-day SMA at $8.45 and the 20-day SMA at $10.02 are both sloping downward right overhead. Even if you zoom into the 4-hour intraday chart, the 20-EMA ($8.63) and 50-SMA ($10.68) remain stacked bearishly above price, and the intraday 4-hour turn indicator is false. Meanwhile, daily RSI sits at 36.68, 4-hour RSI at 39.94, and weekly RSI at 38.37. It is weak, battered, and heavy, yet not even showing a clean climax-volume reversal.

Volume confirms the lack of institutional sponsorship. Friday's 5.42% drop traded 34.57 million shares, just 0.76x the 30-day average volume of 45.26 million shares, while the 10-day average volume has surged to 61.50 million shares during the recent selloff. In institutional tape reading, expanding volume on down weeks followed by lighter volume on bounces—remember KORU bounced +7.41% over the past week after plunging -42.9% over the past month and -65.79% over three months—is classic bear-market distribution, not accumulation. The 14-day Average True Range (ATR) is $1.54—more than 20% of the entire share price in a single average day—with Bollinger Band width stretched to 106.12%.

Let us map the exact price shelves so you know where the structural battlegrounds sit. Above current price ($7.68), immediate resistance sits at the 10-day SMA ($8.45) and 20-day SMA ($10.02), followed by the 10-week EMA ($13.58), the middle pivot ($14.64), the 50-day SMA ($15.85), and Pivot R1 ($19.29). Below current price, the only nearby shelf is the 52-week low at $6.28 and Pivot S1 at $5.99; if that $5.99–$6.28 floor gives way, there is an air pocket all the way down to Pivot S2 at $1.34—territory that historically triggers another Direxion reverse split.

Crucially, this is not just a leverage-wrapper quirk; the underlying unleveraged South Korea ETF (EWY) sits in Stage 1 (Basing) at $142.78, trading 18.61% below its 30-week SMA ($175.43) and 15.24% below its 50-day SMA ($168.46). And zoom out one level further to the US market regime: the S&P 500 is in an official Correction (below its 50-DMA, with only 47.6% of breadth above the 50-DMA, 42.9% above the 200-DMA, and 6 distribution days in the past 25 sessions). In a Correction regime, high-beta Stage 4 instruments are the very first assets institutions liquidate.

What about options? With 20-day historical volatility at 224.1% and ATM implied volatility at 136.9%, an automated screen might flag options as 'IV cheap.' Do not fall for that optical illusion. Buying naked calls into a Stage 4 downtrend with 20% daily ATR is simply paying time decay to catch a falling anvil. Our options engine shows a conditional Bull Call Spread structure (January 15, 2027 $16.5/$19.5 at $0.05 debit) strictly gated behind WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT_OR_BASE: stand aside at $7.68, and never deploy even $600 of spread risk unless KORU tests $6.28, stabilizes, and builds a base. Right now, the tape says one word: avoid.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Investors love to say 'I am down 34%, I might as well wait for a bounce.' Ask yourself a harder question: if you did not own a single share of KORU today, would you look at a Stage 4 chart 70% below its 30-week average in a Correction market and say 'That is my best idea'? If the answer is no, holding it is just anchoring to your cost basis.

section_takeaway: KORU ($7.68) is in confirmed Stage 4 and unleveraged EWY ($142.78) remains in Stage 1 (Basing) below its 30W SMA amidst a US Correction regime; technicals are CAP_REJECTED with no accumulation.

book_subsections.title: 8.1 Multi-Timeframe Anatomy: Weekly, Daily, and 4-Hour Rejection
paragraphs: On the weekly chart, KORU's 30-week simple moving average at $25.31 has rolled over decisively, and price at $7.68 sits -69.66% below that institutional trendline. On the daily chart, the 50-day SMA ($15.85) is well below the 200-day SMA ($24.08) in a classic death-cross configuration, while price remains pinned beneath both the 10-day SMA ($8.45) and 20-day SMA ($10.02). Even on the 4-hour chart, price cannot sustain a close above its 20-EMA ($8.63). Until price stops making lower lows, builds a multi-week horizontal Stage 1 base above $6.28, and reclaims the 10-week EMA on expanding volume, there is zero technical basis for a long trade.

book_subsections.title: 8.2 Why Options Convexity Still Says Stand Aside at $7.68
paragraphs: Even though KORU's 136.9% ATM implied volatility screens below its 224.1% 20-day realized volatility, options are not a free lunch in Stage 4. Buying out-of-the-money calls at $7.68 exposes you to rapid theta decay if KORU drifts sideways or tests $6.28. Only after a confirmed stabilization at the $6.28 support shelf could a defined-risk Bull Call Spread—such as the January 15, 2027 $16.5/$19.5 spread at a $0.05 debit—ever make sense, because selling the upper $19.5 strike offsets over 60% of daily theta and caps worst-case loss strictly at the debit paid. Today, at $7.68, the disciplined options call is to stay in cash.

book_subsections.title: 8.3 Volume Footprint & The Missing Institutional Accumulation
paragraphs: Look closely at the volume signature behind KORU's recent collapse. Over the past 30 trading days, average daily volume has been 45.26 million shares, yet over the most recent 10 trading days—precisely when KORU plunged through $10 and down toward $6.28—average volume surged to 61.50 million shares. That expansion in 10-day volume during a price breakdown tells us liquidation has been active and forceful. By contrast, on Friday November 13 when KORU fell another 5.42% to $7.68, volume cooled to 34.57 million shares (0.76x the 30-day average), with zero sign of institutional accumulation stepping in to absorb supply.

In a healthy Stage 1-to-Stage 2 reversal, you want to see selling volume dry up completely along a flat floor for several weeks, followed by a sudden 1.5x to 2.5x volume thrust on an up week that drives price cleanly above the 10-week EMA. Right now, KORU has none of those hallmarks. Instead, Bollinger Band width sits at a hyper-expanded 106.12% and daily ATR is $1.54—meaning a routine two-day swing can easily wipe out 30% to 40% of an unhedged buyer's position.

book_subsections.title: 8.4 What a Valid Stage 1-to-Stage 2 Transition Would Require
paragraphs: To be fair to future opportunity, nothing stays in Stage 4 forever. If South Korean semiconductor demand holds firm and global markets exit the current Correction, KORU will eventually form a tradeable bottom. What should you watch for on your checklist before ever putting KORU back on a tactical radar? First, watch EWY ($142.78) rather than KORU: EWY needs to stabilize above its Pivot S1 ($136.50), flatten its 50-day SMA ($168.46), and cross back above its 30-week SMA ($175.43). Second, wait for KORU's 20-day historical volatility to compress from 224.1% down below 90%–100%, because lower realized volatility is what shuts off the quadratic decay engine. Until those two conditions align, patience is free and mistakes are expensive.

book_subsections.title: 8.5 Relative Strength & Why Cross-Market Regime Alignment Matters
paragraphs: Stan Weinstein always insisted that you check the market forest before buying any individual tree. Right now, the US market forest is in a Correction: only 47.6% of stocks sit above their 50-day moving average, 42.9% sit above their 200-day moving average, and institutions have printed six distribution days over the last 25 sessions. Meanwhile, KORU's 1-month performance is -42.9%, its 3-month performance is -65.79%, and its 6-month performance is -79.52%. Buying or holding a Stage 4 leveraged ETF against a declining US tape is swimming upstream against a rip current.

book_subsections.title: 8.6 Why Dead-Cat Bounces Trap Stage 4 Holders
paragraphs: One final warning from the tape: in Stage 4 downtrends, sharp one-week bounces—like KORU's +7.41% bounce over the trailing week—are the primary reason traders fail to exit on time. Because 3x leverage magnifies a routine two-day short-covering rally in Seoul into a double-digit percentage pop in New York, holders convince themselves the bottom is finally in. Yet look at the moving averages overhead: every single rally from $7.68 hits resistance at the 10-day SMA ($8.45), the 20-day SMA ($10.02), the 10-week EMA ($13.58), and the 50-day SMA ($15.85). Unless price reclaims its 30-week SMA ($25.31) on heavy institutional accumulation, Stage 4 bounces are exit liquidity, not new bull markets.
